utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the case number is IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. As usual, could we have the appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Counsel. For the Prosecution, Mrs. Tecla Benjamin and Ekkehard Withopf, together with the case manager, Mrs. Kimberly Fleming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Withopf. And could we have the appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Edina Residovic, counsel; Stephane Bourgon is our co-counsel; and Mirna Milanovic is our legal assistant. We represent General Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And could we have the appearances for Mr. Kubura's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Mr. Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Mr. Mulalic, our legal assistant, represent Mr. Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber would like to greet everyone who is present: The Defence, the Prosecution, and the accused, and the administrative personnel present in the courtroom. Today we will be hearing two witnesses, but there were certain matters that we had to deal with before we hear them. So I'm going to ask the Registrar to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness XB, you've been called here as a witness for the Prosecution. The Prosecution will ask you some questions; they're to your right. The Defence, to your left, will ask you some questions when the Prosecution has finished with its examination. The Judges who are before you, if necessary, might ask you some questions. You will testify about events that you have witnessed, and you must provide complete answers to the questions, to the extent that it is possible. And if you do not understand a question, ask the person who has asked you the question to put it to you again. Have you understood me well? Could the Prosecution start with its examination-in-chief. But I should point out that we also have another witness. And given the time that we have used, I know that you will ask questions in a very efficient manner. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Mr. President. Mr. President, I would appreciate if we could go into closed session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We shall continue in closed session for a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness XB, I'll just refresh your memory. We were at the point --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Now the English booth and the B/C/S booth have a problem with hearing the floor and hearing the protected witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the interpreting services is warning us that we cannot hear either the Prosecution or yourselves, and we are not receiving any translation at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we are going to break and wait --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to break, and we are going to hope that this technical problem will be resolved very quickly. We are adjourned. --- Break taken at 9.49 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. We will continue. We have an hour and 15 minutes for this session. We are going to have a break after that time, after an hour and 15 minutes. We are in open session. Can I ask the registrar to confirm that we are in open session. Yes, we are in open session. That means that the voice and the face are distorted. Prosecution, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness XB, at the interruption, you indicated to the Trial Chamber that the attacks actually began on the 8th of June, 1993. Could you now briefly describe what you heard and saw during those attacks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Shooting started, and we realised that we had been attacked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness XB, do you know by whom you were attacked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: BH Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us how you knew that it was members of the BH Army, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They wore multicoloured uniforms, and they wore green bandannas on their arms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness XB, can you assist the Trial Chamber with the physical appearance of these soldiers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They sported long beards. Among them there were black men and there were also foreign citizens.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell the Trial Chamber for how long did this shooting last.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This shooting lasted for a couple of hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you be able to assist us, if at the time the attack was taking place on you, if there were other simultaneous attacks in other areas as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The attack started simultaneously at Cukle, Brajkovici, Guca Gora, Grahovcici, Rudnik. All these are villages with Croatian population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And in your opinion, how would you describe these attacks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The attacks started by mortar fire, continued with small-arms fire -- rifle fire, that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness XB, did it appear to you that these were ad hoc attacks, or did it appear to you as a well-planned attack? How did it appear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These attacks were well-planned ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the benefit of the Trial Chamber, could you tell us why you said that they were well planned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because within the space of only one day, a lot of Croatian population was expelled from Travnik municipality. The town of Travnik fell that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And during the attack, did you leave the village of Postinje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the attack, we withdrew to Maljine village because we could not stay in Postinje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Bosnian Muslim army advance towards you on your way to Maljine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during that time, did you experience any encounter with the army of any sort?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we did not have any encounters, because we were withdrawing and they were following us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Kindly tell the Trial Chamber where did you go to once you got to Maljine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once we arrived in Maljine, there was a house there. I don't know what to call that house. It was like a headquarters, and it was there in case somebody was wounded. That's where we came. We came to that house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber how many of you were in this group at that time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About ten or so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you be able to assist us with the ethnic background of the members of that group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were all Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you be able to tell the Trial Chamber where were the other members of the original group? Where did they go to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They all arrived in Maljine village. But we were not all together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once you got to the house that you described for us in Maljine, could you tell us who you met there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the house, there were a lot of women, children, elderly people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any wounded people in this house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness XB, did there come a time when anybody asked you to surrender?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The BH Army was on surrounding -- on the surrounding hills. We couldn't stay there, and we simply had to surrender.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you surrender?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A lady put up a white flag through a window, and that's how we surrendered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us what transpired after you surrendered.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After we surrendered, the soldiers put their arms in one place. Then the BH Army troops came, and they separated women and children from the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you say that these soldiers were soldiers of the 7th Muslim Brigade of the BiH Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, according to the transcript, the witness didn't mention the 7th Muslim Brigade in his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are right. He has answered, but he never mentioned the 7th Brigade. He has mentioned the BH Army, the Muslim army, but the 7th Brigade has never been mentioned in the testimony so far. So your objection is correct. It doesn't appear in the transcript. Can you please rephrase your question, and bear in mind that the witness has never mentioned the 7th Brigade up to now.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: My apologies, Mr. President. I stand corrected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, why do you say that the soldiers were members of the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because in Travnik municipality and the entire area, there was the 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this time, Witness, were you able to recognise any other army personnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this stage the Judges would like to ask you how come you recognised these people as members of the 7th Brigade? What made you think that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They had insignia. They had patches on their uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you could tell by the patches, by the insignia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Much obliged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Having surrendered, did the BH Army soldiers do anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that moment, they didn't do anything, when we were surrendering. They didn't do anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the surrender was completed, did you go anywhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the surrender was completed, they told us to start walking towards Mehurici, Mehurici village, both columns, the columns containing women and children and the other column containing men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber what position were you in the column.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was at the end of my column.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Witness XB, can you describe for the Trial Chamber what you were wearing at that time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had a pair of jeans, a red shirt, and a vest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, Witness XB, did you belong to any army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I was 15 at the time. I couldn't belong to any army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us approximately how many people were in this column.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 160, I think, women, children, and able-bodied men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you be able to assist us with approximately what was the ethnicity, approximately, of the members of the column?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were all Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that point, Witness XB, where did you think that you were being escorted to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that moment, I thought we were being escorted to Mehurici, because at the school there was some sort of headquarters or something. I don't know what.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On your way, were you stopped at any point? And if so, by whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were stopped. Somebody ordered us to stop. A group of soldiers was coming towards us from the direction of Mehurici. I don't know how many of them were there in the group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to recognise this group of soldiers, Witness XB?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you assist the Court with the distance between Bikose and Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I can't tell you. I never travelled that distance before this event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. At any time, Witness XB, on your journey to Mehurici were you interrupted in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We were told to stop. And when we stopped, the soldiers that were coming towards us told the last column to turn around, and they took the women and the children towards Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Kindly tell the Trial Chamber where were you taken to, you and the members of your group.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were taken to Bikose village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you arranged in any particular way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were walking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you have just said that you were taken to Bikose village. A little while ago you said that you were 15 at that time. Which group did you belong to, the group which contained women and children or the group which contained able-bodied men? Where did you belong to at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we were captured, that's how we were separated. Men were put on one side; women and children were put on the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what group were you put with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was put in the group with the men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have ordered protective measures, so you -- so the name of the cousin has to be expunged from the transcript, because this could serve to identify the witness. So can you order this to be done. May we continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Much obliged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at any point in time while you were walking did you receive a command to stop?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you stopped at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we didn't stop at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us what transpired while you were walking along the road to Bikose.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As we were walking towards Bikose, we were walking normally. We didn't -- were not allowed to look around too much. There were troops around us. Our heads were bowed down.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think we may need to go into closed session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Can we go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: During this time, could you describe for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Registrar has to confirm that we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During this time, could you describe for the Trial Chamber how you felt.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I felt confused, afraid. I don't know. I felt exasperated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you, Witness XB, tell the Trial Chamber what happened on your arrival to Bikose.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we arrived in the village of Bikose, we carried on walking normally, and all of a sudden they started shooting at us. I lied down on the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us what you mean when you say "they started shooting at us." Could you tell us who you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm referring to the members of the BH Army and the foreigners who were with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us how close the members of the BH Army were to you when all this shooting was going on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were about 15 or 20 metres away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you tell us for how long did this shooting last.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Several minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the end of the shooting, what did you and the members of your group do?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We're in open session again, so in line 6 and 7 it's necessary to redact the reference to a relative. I note that in the English version no reference is made, whereas there was an explicit reference in the French translation. So I assume that what the witness said in B/C/S was translated into French, but it doesn't appear in the English version. So no reference is made in the English version; whereas, I heard the reference in French. So the witness must have made a reference to his relative in his language. I draw the attention of the Defence so this fact. So it is necessary to redact this reference from the B/C/S and French version. In the English version, this reference is not made. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We have the same problem again. Again, in the English version, no reference is made to the relative; whereas, in the French version, this reference was made. I assume that he must have said this in the B/C/S version, or not, unless the French interpreter has added something. Nothing has been added; very well. The interpreter has stated that the witness did mention his relative, so it should be redacted from the B/C/S and French version.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Much obliged, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go anywhere at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I stood up. Once I'd got up, we jumped over a wall half a metre high, perhaps, and we hid behind two houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us where these houses were.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we got up -- well, the houses were in that village, the village of Bikose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you move from the village of Bikose?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We set off from the village of Bikose, the five of us. We descended to the village of Postinje. And from the village of Postinje, we descended to the Bila River. That's what it's called. There was some kind of a trench there, and the young men who were all wounded -- well, we all went to that trench to bandage ourselves, to put bandages on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think we may have to go into closed session at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Registrar, can we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, for appearing for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, this is the examination-in-chief of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. As the Trial Chamber has a few questions to ask, we'll go back into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence may now commence its cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. XB. My name is Edina Residovic, and I am Defence counsel for General Hadzihasanovic. As the Presiding Judge has already told you, I will be asking you some questions. I would be grateful if you could answer them. And whenever I mention a fact that might in any way help to identify you, I will attempt to go into private session. First of all, I would like you to answer a number of general questions. Would it be correct to say that you've already given a number of statements about everything that you experienced on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the last statement which you gave -- that last statement was given to investigators from the OTP in the year 2000 and 2001; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to that statement --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we first go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the night between the 7th and the 8th of July, together with some 30 villagers, you were in an old house which was used as the gathering place for those people who participated in the defence of the village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: About 20 armed villagers were members of the first shift. They went to their positions, and the rest of you remained in the house. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you heard shots early in the morning, you took your rifle and went to a trench; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't have a rifle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am turning towards the Defence. The interpretation that I received in French, you asked him whether he took his rifle up. To that moment, he'd never said that he had a rifle. Maybe you should have asked him whether he had a rifle, whether he was armed as a member of the defence of the village. In his answer, he answered, "I didn't have a rifle." So can you rephrase and continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you for your remark. In my cross-examination, I am putting it to the witness to confirm something that he already mentioned in his statement. That's why I put my question in the way that I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, I don't have this statement in front of me, so when you ask your questions, I don't know why you're asking it. I don't have the context that you have.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The witness answered as he did. I'm not going to confront him with his statement. I shall move on with my questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that earlier you had dugout trenches around your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't dig anything. Others did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that all of you from that house went to the trenches from which you put up strong defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Once you ran out of ammunition, a decision was made for all of you to withdraw towards Maljine, which is about 2 or 3 kilometres away from your village and is behind a hill that is between these two villages; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Because of the hills that surround your village, you found it very difficult to see what was going on in the general area from the positions where you found yourself at the time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The only thing that you could see from your position was that there were sounds of small arms coming from all directions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. And I could also see smoke.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So apart from the smoke, you did not see any combat activities in any other part of the general area of your village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Earlier in your testimony, when you said that the BH Army had attacked Guca Gora, Ovnak, Grahovcici, and other villages, it was just an assumption. You only learnt that later on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. But we didn't attack ourselves, did we?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have only four minutes left before the next break. That means that you're going to put a number of questions and then you're going to continue after the break. Very well, then. Can we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. XB, you have told us that at one point you withdrew to a trench. You stayed in the trench putting up fierce resistance until the moment the BH Army approached --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are still in private session. We are moving into open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. XB, you have told us that at one point you withdrew from the old house to a trench, from which you put up fierce resistance. My question is as follows: You stayed in the trench until the moment BH Army troops approached some 100 -- a couple hundred metres away from you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After that, you started walking across the hill towards Gornje Maljine, and this decision was made by Predrag Puselja, who was the leader of your group; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived at the top of the hill which separates Postinje from Gornje Maljine, you saw that BH Army troops were already in Gornje Maljine; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before that, because of the distance at which BH Army troops were and because of the fierce fire that you were exposed, to you couldn't recognise exactly which troops were in question. You only assumed that those were BH Army troops. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: From the top of that hill, you also saw that one part of Gornje Maljine was still not occupied, and that's where you headed off with your column; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: There was a makeshift surgery there, so some of the soldiers from your group entered that makeshift surgery; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: BH Army troops asked you to surrender your weapons. You said that one woman waved a white flag as a sign that you were surrendering. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That woman --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, can we have please go to private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Do you have any questions for this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, given that the witness has answered Mrs. Residovic's question and said that he wasn't familiar with the organisation and structure of the BH Army and that he wasn't familiar with the insignia of the BH Army, the Defence for Mr. Kubura has no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does the Prosecution have any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, there'll be no re-examination for this witness at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness XB, thank you for having come to The Hague and for having answered the questions put to you by the Prosecution and the Defence. You have also answered questions put to you by the Judges. We wish you a good trip home. The usher will escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll turn to the Prosecution. We have another witness now?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, Your Honours, we have another witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Protective measures have been requested for this witness; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours. This is the witness we discussed the protective measures yesterday evening, and the protective measures have been granted as requested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Registrar, protective measures have been granted for this second witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that as part of the protective measures we will be using a pseudonym; there will be voice distortion and facial distortion. Could you please remind us of the protective measures that were requested.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honours, we requested assignment of pseudonym. We requested facial distortion. However, we did not request voice distortion. And the Chamber granted pseudonym and facial distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we will be using a pseudonym and there will be facial distortion. As far as the technical measures are concerned, there shouldn't be any problems, since we've already had facial distortion for the previous witness. So the technical measures taken should be the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll call the witness into the courtroom, but we will go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness XC, you will now have to answer the questions put to you by the Prosecution over to your right. After they have concluded their examination-in-chief, the Defence for the accused, who are to your left, will also ask you some questions and the three Judges, who are before you, may ask you questions, if necessary. Try to answer the questions as extensively as possible. And if there is a question that you fail to understand, ask the person who is putting the question to you to ask you the question again. It's 12.33. We'll be working until 1.45 without a break. So if the Prosecution wants to avoid calling this witness tomorrow, I would like to ask the Prosecution to proceed rapidly, to the extent that this is possible. Otherwise, the witness will have to appear tomorrow. Mr. Withopf, you may take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, it can be anticipated that the examination-in-chief will not last longer than 1 hour and 30 minutes. However, anticipating some questions in cross-examination, I think it cannot be avoided to recall this witness tomorrow morning. I will, however, focus my question -- my questions to the highest extent possible. May I please ask you, Mr. President, to go back in private session, since the likely answers to my very first questions may contain some identifying features.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness XC, did there come a time when you noticed foreigners arriving in the area you used to live in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That's something I noticed around the month of July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: These foreigners you noticed arriving in the month of July 1992, what sort of foreigners were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the whole, they were from Arab countries. They were different from us. We would see them at the market in Mehurici when we went there, but on the whole they were from Arab countries.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: They were different from you. Can you please go into some sort of more detail. What were the differences?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the colour of their skin was different and the clothes they wore on the whole. When they would go to the market, they were wearing these long robes, white ones and black ones. Those sort of things. That was at the beginning, when they first started arriving.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness XC, after you noticed them arriving, do you know where these foreigners were living?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most of these foreigners that arrived in my village stayed in Serbian houses, as far as I know. Those Serbs had moved out, and the village was Poljanice. Many came and got married very quickly, and that's how they found their accommodation. In any case, they were concentrated in Gornje Poljanice village while we were still in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were these foreigners also seen in Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. At that time, I would often take my mother-in-law to Travnik to the hospital there, and I would see them around the hospital in Travnik. We saw them in various places. Everybody who resided in the area could see them. They didn't hide their presence. Everybody knew that they were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At that point in time, was there a certain word you used in order to refer to such foreigners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We used the term that the local Bosniak Muslims gave them. They called them Mujahedins. I didn't know what the meaning of that word was. I believe that it means a holy warrior or something like that. Before that, I didn't even hear this name.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were mentioning just a few seconds ago that you have seen many of such Mujahedin in the area of Mehurici and also in the area of Travnik. Can you please inform the Trial Chamber in more detail about the number of such Mujahedin you have seen arriving in mid of 1992 in that area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the beginning, there were not many of them arriving. I wouldn't be able to give you the exact number, because I was never aware that I would ever have to discuss that in this place here. However, as the conflict progressed, as the war progressed, their numbers increased.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: These Mujahedin, did they have arms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They had pistols and automatic rifles. I would like to add to that that while I was detained - it occurred to me to only mention this yesterday - we detainees worked. And at one point a group of Mujahedins came. One of them had a sword which he was waving some 30 or 40 metres away from us. And that was already when -- during the time of conflict. Up to that moment, I had never seen that kind of a weapon. It was some sort of a short sword.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: These Mujahedin, did they wear uniforms or something similar to a uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They wore uniforms. They wore white robes. Some had uniforms. It varied.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Mujahedin in Mehurici, what did they do in 1992 after they had arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Having arrived in Mehurici, these Mujahedins rallied local Muslim population around themselves, asking them to join their movement. They had training in the village. We had problems with that, because my village, Postinje, is in such a position that there is no other road through the village but the road leading to our village. They would come to our village, the locals and the Mujahedins. There would be two or three Mujahedins and the local Muslims would be running after them shouting "Tekbir, Allah." They would be passing through the village. I don't know what their intent was when they were passing through the village. I didn't see any need for them going through the village. Our local guys took some of the people from some international organisations to a place above Mehurici, where they were in training. The local young Bosniak and Muslims who wanted to join their group were trained. I know a colleague of mine from work. His son, who was not even 18 when he joined the movement, was killed while he was fighting on their side. This is the kind of people that these Mujahedins took under their wing.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness XC, you were telling us that the Mujahedin had training in the village. What sort of training are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They would just run through the village. They would go to the far end of the village. And then they would come back. It was probably some sort of physical training. Why did they choose a Croat village to run through it? One could only guess. And I believe that this was just to intimidate the population who resided in that village. There were other villages which would have been much more conducive to their training than our village, with only one road through it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This training you are detailing, do you recall the time as to when it actually happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first time this happened was in September, and then a neighbour of mine and I went to the police to ask them to prevent that, because people were scared. However, this continued for a while. And later on, I remember that I was on my way to the defence line on Mount Vlasic. It was in the morning. And again, I heard shouts through the village. This could have been in February of the same year. So they started their exercises to the village again.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: For clarification, the village you are referring to, which one is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness XC, moving on to April and May 1993, how would you describe the relationship between the Croats and the -- the Croats, on the one-hand side, and the Muslims, on the other-hand side, in the area your military unit was based at this point in time? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To be honest, up to that moment the relationship was not bad. This is all very close. In April 1993, together with my squad, I was on my way to the line on Mount Vlasic, and we were together, us and the BH Army. This was the line facing the Serbs. And around the 11th of April we received our information that the bridge in Sarici had been mined. Since there are very few of us in the village, a colleague of mine and I were ordered to go back to the village and stand guard because the situation had already -- getting to be rather complicated at the time. From that moment up to the moment of the first conflict, we had village guards to provide security for the village. And up to the moment of the open conflict, there were minor provocations from their side. We complained, to no avail.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You're making reference to the moment the conflict started. When actually did the conflict start?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The conflict started on the 8th of June. And I'm referring to the attack on our village and other villages. Three days before that, some Croat houses in Barici village were set on fire. This village had been abandoned. Nobody was guarding it. One night one stable was set on fire and then a house, a house whose owner was Franjo Bobas. And then a day or two before the open conflict, they started opening sniper fire on our village. On the 5th or 6th of June, a villager from another village was wounded on the way to my house. He was not armed. It was in the morning. They opened fire on him. He was wounded in the leg, and he lost his leg. The real conflict, the attack, started about half past 3.00 in the morning. I was standing guard until 3.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness XC, we will come to these details in a few seconds, please. You're making reference to the 8th of June. Just for clarification, are we talking about the 8th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is the year.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. And you were mentioning that a few days prior to the 8th of June, 1993 "they started sniper fire." Do you have any knowledge as to who "they" actually were?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: (redacted). From those trenches, they opened sniper fire. They could have been either locals or somebody else. They were standing guard there. They were the ones who opened sniper fire. We couldn't see them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were mentioning, Witness XC, that the real conflict, the attack started about half past 3.00 in the morning. What day are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was on the 8th of June, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And where have you been at this point in time on the 8th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was on duty, standing guard up to 3.00 in the morning. Then I went to catch a short nap. I was replaced by my father. He woke me up about half past 3.00. He told me that we were to withdraw because an attack had started and that we were to withdraw towards Maljine village.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. And where have you been on duty at 3.00 in the morning? In which area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in my village, by my house. I was patrolling. That's all we did. That was our duty. We patrolled the village. We did not have any trenches in my village. We only had one trench above my village, and that was just in case of an attack, to be able to pull out the civilians. And that was all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session, and the name of your village might identify you. I'm going to ask Mr. Registrar to have this name redacted from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the 8th of June, 1993, at 3.00 in the morning, do you know which army attacked your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I arrived in Maljine, our village had been attacked from the direction of Mehurici. I wasn't able to tell which army was there at the time, but I believe that it was the 306th Mountain Brigade together with the 7th Muslim Brigade. Because it was not only my village that had been attacked but also the villages of Orasac, Cukle, Grahovcici, Bukovica, Guca Gora, Radonjici, Rudnik, Rudnik Bila, Podovi; all of the villages which had been inhabited by Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The two military units you were just referring to - namely, the 306th Mountain Brigade and the 7th Muslim Brigade - to which army did they belong to on the 8th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most probably to the BH Army. I don't know whether the 7th Corps had already been established. I was -- I am not aware of that. And as for this mountain brigade, whether it belonged to the Zenica Corps, I wouldn't know. They are probably -- not probably, as a matter of fact. They are most certainly parts of the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: For clarification, Witness XC: So the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade and the 306th Mountain Brigade were for certain part of the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What made you believe, Witness XC, that it was the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade and the 306th Mountain Brigade which was attacking the area you were just describing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because the headquarters of the 306th Brigade was in Mehurici, and this is where the attack was launched from. This brigade was mostly composed by people from Krajina who had been expelled from Banja Luka, Prijedor. So refugees and locals who belonged to the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were just mentioning that you were forced to retreat, forced by the BiH army. Whilst you were retreating, did you hear the members of the BiH army shouting anything? And if so, what did they shout?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I withdrew towards Maljine. I saw the village of Bikose, a Croat village, on fire. They arrived as far as our position, ask they shouted "Tekbir," "Allah-U-Ekber," and similar things. I waited for my father there. I saw that I couldn't pass through there. I lowered myself down. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did there come a time, Witness XC, when you have been arrested on the 8th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was sometime in the afternoon, around 2.00, when the situation quietened down. It had started raining. After 2.00, they started walking through the village. I noticed a group coming towards the cowshed. There were three or four young men in the group. Among them was an acquaintance of mine, a Bosniak, a Muslim. Together with my father, we decided not to shoot but, rather, to surrender.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please briefly describe, Witness XC, as to how you surrendered.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I called out to them. I shouted at them, "We are here. We are willing to surrender." And then this acquaintance of mine, whose name I mentioned while I was shouting, he told us, "Come out with your hands up in the air. Throw out your weapons." (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please inform the Trial Chamber as to whom you surrendered, meaning the army to which you surrendered, and if you know, the military unit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew this guy. They had white bandannas around their heads. They were probably members of the BH Army. One of them wore the insignia of the 7th Muslim Brigade, so I assume that all of them were members of that brigade. Later on another man from the group, a neighbour of mine whom I didn't recognise at first, told me later on that they were BH Army members. The guy who bore the 7th Brigade insignia, whether he was its member or not, I don't know, because in our parts everybody could wear any uniform. There was no law and order that forbade that. On one of the members of the BH Army, I even saw a helmet with a chequer-board insignia that he must have taken from one of our fallen soldiers. It was very hard to know just looking at people which unit they belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After you surrendered, what did happen to you and the others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we came out of the cowshed, one of them started provoking us. He started shouting, "They should be killed." And this guy, whom I knew, wouldn't allow the others to do that. They escorted us through the Croatian village. And as we were in the middle of Donje Maljine, which was a Bosniak Muslim village, we came as far as that. And then a man with somewhat darker skin was waiting for us there. At first I thought that he was a Mujahedin, because he sported a long beard and he bore the insignia of the 7th Muslim Brigade. He was from Bukovica. He started beating me. I still have a scar. And then my father shouted, "Don't do that. He is a father of several children." Some other people came to my rescue. And then this guy stopped beating me. Later on I learned that his name was Hadzija and that he was from Bukovica village. From there they took us to a building which was still under construction. This building had a garage. This is a building in Maljine which is currently inhabited by the local hodza. This is where they took us and they kept us there for a while. Soldiers who would enter that building would beat us and kick us. Some of them did; some didn't. Then our neighbours realised that we were not safe there, and then they took us into the Prcanovic house, to the basement of that house, and this is where we came under the protection of one of our neighbours. He was to protect us until the moment our further destiny would be decided.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who was actually taking you from the one house to the next house, and who was making the decisions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a man called Taracija. He also had a beard. He told us to find a better shelter, to avoid any bigger problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you have been brought to Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This was about 4.00 or 5.00. A car came by. It was a TAM with a canvas cover. They gave us two escorts, and they transported us towards Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Once you arrived in Mehurici on the 8th of June, 1993, where have you been brought to?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can I just interrupt you here for a second, Witness XC.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I'm now going to show Witness XC via Sanction a photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness XC, do you see a photograph on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it. That's the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: For the record, this is Prosecution Exhibit P28.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what you can see on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can see the primary school in Mehurici, from the front.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is this the Mehurici Elementary School you have been brought to at the evening of the 8th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were mentioning a sports hall. Was it the sports hall of this Mehurici Elementary School?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I'm now going to show via Sanction Witness XC a further photograph. This photograph is Prosecution Exhibit P29.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness XC, can you please inform the Trial Chamber what you can see on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can see the sports hall of the primary school in Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is this the sports hall you have been brought to on 8th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's where we -- that's where they took me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you voluntarily go to this sports hall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't. They simply took us to the sports hall. And as I have said a while ago, there were over 200 civilians, women, children, elderly people, and so on. They were all civilians who had been taken captive in Maljine.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were mentioning the names -- not the names, sorry -- the number of the people which you found in this sports hall. Is it your recollection about 200 persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps 200. Perhaps more. Something like that. But the hall was full.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The about 200 persons you've seen in the sports hall of the Mehurici Elementary School, did they volunteer to be in the Mehurici Elementary School?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. None of us volunteered to go there. These people all surrendered. They were mostly civilians. There were some soldiers too. But most of the soldiers suffered the fate that they suffered. They were taken to this sports hall. Some people stayed on. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's necessary to redact line 17, which would make it possible to identify the witness, since he has mentioned his grandfather.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Once you arrived at the Mehurici Elementary School, did you notice anything at the building of the Mehurici Elementary School?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, at the beginning, at the front of the school there was a big black Mujahedin flag on this window here, and lower down there was -- there were some beams, wooden beams that had been placed there as protection from mines or grenades, something like that. And on the third window here, there was a black flag. There must have been some sort of a Mujahedin command there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We're still in open session. It would have been better if we had gone into private session. So let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We're in open session. Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I please suggest to go back in private session, since I wish to inform both the Trial Chamber and Defence counsel about the witness schedule for tomorrow, Thursday, and Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll go back into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 21st day of January, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.48 p.m.,
